args.text: [lane-tern] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to a server that has moved or been retired, so pages fail or time out. (2) Slow recovery: when a site switches to a backup server after a failure, cached answers keep traffic going to the broken one. (3) Security exposure: a forged or hijacked answer stays in the cache and keeps misleading users long after the problem is fixed.

args.text: [lane-tern] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail in ways that leave you unsure whether a request worked, so the sender must be able to try again safely. If repeating a request gives the same result as sending it once, a retry cannot cause harm such as a double payment or a duplicate order.

args.text: [lane-tern] UUIDv7 (version 7 of the Universally Unique Identifier) has two trade-offs as a primary key. (1) Gain: ids start with a timestamp, so new rows land near the end of the index, which keeps inserts fast and tidy compared with fully random ids. (2) Cost: each id is 16 bytes, larger than a plain 4 or 8 byte integer, so indexes grow. The embedded time also leaks when a row was created, and ids made in the same millisecond may not be strictly ordered unless the generator takes care.

args.text: [lane-tern] A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it alters the main data files, so the record survives a crash or power cut. After a restart, the database replays the log to recover finished changes and undo unfinished ones, which keeps the data consistent.

args.text: [lane-tern] (1) Fair comparison: if the client version changes between runs, a difference in results could come from the client rather than the thing being measured, so pinning keeps only one variable changing. (2) Repeatability: others can rerun the benchmark later and get comparable results, because updates to the client cannot silently change speed or behaviour.

args.text: [lane-tern] Backpressure is a signal from a queue that is filling up, telling the senders to slow down or wait, so that the queue does not overflow or use up all the memory. It works by making producers pause, drop work or be refused when consumers cannot keep pace, which keeps the whole system steady.

args.text: [lane-tern] Two ways a cron job (a scheduled task) can run twice: (1) the same schedule is installed on two servers, so both fire at the same moment; (2) a slow run is still going when the next scheduled start arrives, so the runs overlap. One guard: take a lock before starting, for example a lock file or a database lock, and exit at once if another run already holds it.

args.text: [lane-tern] A tombstone is a small marker that records that an item was deleted, instead of removing the item outright. In a replicated store (one that keeps copies on several machines) it stops a copy that missed the delete from sending the old item back to the others. Tombstones are cleared away only after every copy has seen them, which is usually after a set waiting period.

[lane-tern] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code with no change in between, so a plain re-run often gives a different result. (2) The failures are tied to timing, order or the environment, such as waiting on a clock, running after another test, or relying on a shared network or file. A genuinely failing test fails the same way every time.

args.text: [lane-tern] A lease-based lock grants ownership only until a set time, so it depends on every machine agreeing what the time is. Clock skew (machines disagreeing about the time) means a holder may think its lease is still valid after the lock service has expired it and given it to someone else. Two owners then act at once, which is the very thing the lock should prevent.
